$comment: The board's words. Images come from the capture; everything a person reads
Kept as data next to the capture script, not inside the generator, for the
reason capture_screens_web.mjs gives for parsing screen names out of the
harness: anything that names a screen twice drifts. The generator fails
loudly if a key here is missing from the capture or vice versa, so this file
cannot quietly fall behind the app.
CODES ARE PINNED, NOT POSITIONAL. Each screen carries its own, and the
generator only checks that it is unique and starts with its act's letter.
Adding a screen means giving it the next free number in its act; nothing
already on the board moves. Prose refers to other plates as {{key}} and the
generator substitutes the code, so a reference cannot go stale either.
host — shell: a tab root, so nav bar and coach mark are both on it
pushed: a full screen over the shell, with a back affordance
sheet: a modal bottom sheet, dismissed by drag or scrim
dialog: an alert, dismissed by its own buttons
in/out/next follow docs/navigation.md, which is the audit these answer to.
since: the logging rework, with saved workouts that start filled and learn at Finish, backup that says where it stands, and every past session editable; the purchase sheet; and a rest timer that reaches a locked phone. Every other screen was restyled in the same pass, with glass bars and sheets and spring motion, so look at the older plates too

acts.title: Signing in
acts.lede: Tracking is never gated, so the app opens usable and an account is optional. Nothing here is on the way to the gym — these two screens exist only because somebody asked for something that needs a server, and the pending count is the argument for it. It names what is at stake on this device rather than asserting that syncing is good.

acts.title: Track — now
acts.sub: The tab the app opens on, and the whole free half
acts.lede: "Track", not "Home": in Run the front page is a summary of the day; here it is the thing you are actually doing in the gym, and the label should say so. One primary button, whose verb is decided by what the plan and the recorder have to say. The coach mark sits bottom-right on this and every other tab — the shell reserves that room, which is why a screenshot without it is a screenshot of a build nobody ships.

acts.title: A workout, start to finish
acts.sub: The only flow in the app that is really a flow
acts.lede: One screen replaces another here, and the summary is where it ends rather than a detour off it. Every set is written the moment it is ticked, which is what makes backing out safe, an interrupted session resumable, and Finish a replacement rather than a push — back must never return to a session that has ended.

acts.title: Plan — ahead
acts.sub: Behind the entitlement, and the paywall is the empty state
acts.lede: The offer is the tab's own empty state rather than a wall in front of it, so what is being sold and where it will appear are the same screen. Past it: no week number, no end date, no completion. Those are marathon ideas, and "get stronger" has no week 12 — the week is derived from weekdays rather than scheduled into, which is why a rest day here is an answer and not a gap.

acts.title: The coach
acts.sub: A sheet over where you were, never a fourth destination
acts.lede: The mark floats over all three tabs (Run's ADR-0017): a dock lives inside one tab and would put the coach on a third of the app. Opening it checks the account and the entitlement before the message rather than after, so a refusal never arrives on a screen with no route to the thing that would fix it. What opens is a sheet over the surface you were on — you can still see where you were, which is the difference between asking about this and leaving to go and ask.

racks.title: Where a conversation goes when it ends
Judged in a bubble, not in a table

acts.title: The intake, end to end
acts.sub: Four questions behind the paywall, and what the coach does with them
acts.lede: This act carried a flag on every plate in it until 2026-08-28. planning/domain/intake_flow.dart defined seven questions with their own controls and a step count, and it was imported by its own test and the preview harness — nothing else. What shipped was bubbles and a composer. The gap is now closed in the direction the storage allowed. Four of the seven land in PlanIntake, which persists, and those are built — these plates are PlanIntakeScreen itself rather than a fake transcript in a coach sheet. The other three are body facts that docs/coach-profile.md puts in core, and core has nowhere to put them: no body_metrics, no height_cm, no year_of_birth in any migration. They were three plates of a conversation the backend could not record, so they are cut rather than rendered and discarded. The wheel that asks them is built and ships in the coach — what is missing is a table, not a control. The last two plates stay flagged, and say what for.

racks.title: Ordered by leverage, not by convention

acts.title: Progress — behind
acts.sub: The log, the year, and one photograph a week
acts.lede: The third tab, and the one a new account has nothing to put in — so its empty state shows the shape of what is coming rather than collapsing to a line of apology. Photos are one stream per pose at one photograph a week, and the cadence is the feature: a body does not change between Tuesday and Wednesday, and an app that accepts a photo a day teaches the wrong habit. Four plates here had never been photographed before this board.

acts.title: Account and settings
acts.sub: Pushed from Profile's gear — nothing here is on a tab
acts.lede: Units are device-first and account-second: the device half is what makes them survive a launch at all, since tracking needs no sign-in, and the account half is what makes them agree with Run. The account reports rather than reassures — nothing here blocks logging, and signing out is "stop syncing", not "erase my training". The coach's memory is deliberately separate from the coach: somebody who has stopped paying should still be able to read what was stored about them and delete it.

acts.title: Privacy, legal and leaving
acts.sub: Pushed from Settings › Privacy & legal — the surface a reviewer goes looking for
acts.lede: Liftio's changelog is a list of rejections bought once, and this act is where they are not bought twice. All six plates landed on 2026-09-01 and not one had ever been photographed, which made them the largest blind spot on the board: the part of the app most likely to be the reason it is rejected was the part with no picture of it. The documents render from bundled copy rather than a fetch, so they are readable offline and cannot change under the person who agreed to them, and a staleness test pins each one to its file in docs/. Every one still carries a draft, legally unreviewed banner — legal review is a real open item, not a formality.

settings-coach.title: Settings — the coach switch
settings-coach.in: {{settings-signed-in}} › a build with a coach in it
settings-coach.next: Turn the coach off, or open the disclosure beside it
settings-coach.note: The section the other four Settings plates were missing.
settings-coach.doc: useCoach and deleter are both null-hides-the-control, and not one of the four Settings plates passed either — so the Coach heading, the switch, the disclosure row beside it and the route to deletion rendered on no plate at all. The whole of the 2026-09-01 compliance work was invisible to the board that exists to prove it is there.

settings-coach-off.title: Settings — coach off
settings-coach-off.doc: The subtitle stops naming OpenRouter in the present tense, and the mark leaves every other surface — which is what makes this a consent control rather than a display preference. It is device-local for the same reason: an account row is something a restore could quietly flip back on. Building a plan is an AI request too, so the switch had to reach _canPlan, or Plan would have gone on sending the intake answers — injury notes included — with the coach switched off.

legal.title: Privacy & legal
legal.next: Any of the three documents, or leave
legal.note: The one place the compliance surfaces are reachable from.
legal.doc: Three data-rights documents kept together rather than scattered through Settings, and deliberately the same shape as run's, so the two apps do not present compliance differently. The email at the top says which account the rights below apply to — which is also how somebody signed in as the wrong address finds out.

legal-signed-out.title: Privacy & legal — no account
legal-signed-out.note: The deletion row is absent, not disabled.
legal-signed-out.doc: Both halves of deletion are null and the row is gone entirely. An app that cannot delete an account should not offer to, and Guideline 5.1.1(v) only applies where one can be created in the first place. This is the state a reviewer reaches first, because tracking has never needed a sign-in.

terms.title: Terms of use
terms.doc: Rendered from structure rather than markdown, so it takes the app's own typography, needs no parser, and cannot silently change under the person who agreed to it. The source of truth is docs/terms-of-use.md and a staleness test pins the load-bearing sentences to it. This is also where the auto-renew disclosure has to be written when payments land — a test currently fails if anybody writes half of it.

privacy.title: Privacy policy
privacy.doc: One parameterised screen rather than run's three near-identical classes: nothing about rendering the policy differs from rendering the terms, and three classes is three places for a padding change to be applied twice and forgotten once.

ai-disclosure.title: How your coach uses AI
ai-disclosure.in: {{legal}} › also the mark in {{coach}}, and beside the switch in {{settings-coach}}
ai-disclosure.note: Reachable from three places, on purpose.
ai-disclosure.doc: Guideline 5.1.2(i), and more acute here than it was for Liftio, which sent numerical aggregates only — Lift sends the lifter's own words about their body and injuries to OpenRouter. Names the provider, what is sent, and what is not. The affordance sits in the coach sheet's top bar and shows mid-intake as well as in conversation, because the questionnaire is where the injury notes are typed.

delete-account.title: Delete account
delete-account.out: App bar back, until it has happened
delete-account.note: Opens on the narrower scope, disarmed.
delete-account.doc: Guideline 5.1.1(v). One login serves the whole suite, so "delete my account" names two different requests and the app has to ask which — run offers neither and sends no scope at all, which the function reads as everything. The narrow choice still cannot promise the login survives, and this screen says so before the tap rather than after it: if Run holds nothing, a profile with nothing behind it is not kept on somebody's behalf.
delete-account.flag: The done state is not on this board. It exists only after a typed phrase and a tap, so the harness cannot address it without faking a state the code cannot reach. Both scopes were proved against the deployed function on 2026-09-01 instead.

sign-in.title: Sign in
sign-in.out: App bar back — blocked while a sign-in is in flight
sign-in.next: Sign in, or create an account
sign-in.note: Nine sessions waiting to back up, named rather than implied.
sign-in.doc: Reached, never launched into: tracking needs no account, so this screen only ever opens because somebody asked for something that does. The pending count is the argument — it names what is at stake on this device rather than asserting that syncing is good. Back is blocked mid-request because the call completes either way and would otherwise report into a screen that is gone.

sign-in-error.title: Sign in — rejected
sign-in-error.next: Correct the field and try again
sign-in-error.note: The error sits with the field, not in a banner at the top.
sign-in-error.doc: The failure is rendered against the input that caused it rather than as a banner, so the fix and the complaint are in one place. Nothing is cleared: a typo in a password should not cost you the email you typed correctly.

track.title: Track
track.out: Nav bar — no back, correctly; nothing sits above a tab root
track.note: Three figures, the log, and the mark. Where a free account lives.
track.doc: "Track", not "Home": in Run the front page is a summary of the day, here it is the thing you are actually doing in the gym, and the label should say so. This is the state a free account sits in permanently — no plan, no open session, one primary button. The coach mark is bottom-right on this and every other tab, which is what the shell reserves the room above the nav bar for.

path.note: The room for the mark is reserved by the thing that knows whether there is a mark. Each surface reserving it itself meant dead space above the nav bar whenever the coach was absent, and three places to keep in step.

Indexed rather than rebuilt, so switching tabs keeps each surface's scroll position and in-flight state. The shell holds the units, so a change in Settings reaches Track and Profile without either reloading.
One controller for both entry points — plain start and planned start — so the resume rule cannot be implemented twice and drift.
Resume beats start, always. The open session is offered back rather than replaced, which is what makes walking away from the gym safe.
A push, not a replacement: Track is still underneath, and backing out lands on it with the session still open.
Refreshed on return as well as via onDone. Backing out with the session still open must leave Track offering to resume it, and onDone only fires when it ended.

track-coach.title: Track — the coach has something
track-coach.in: Nav bar › Track, with an unread note
track-coach.note: The unread dot, and nothing else changed.
track-coach.doc: The only difference from {{track}} is the dot on the mark, which is the entire reason both plates exist. The mark is a mark and not a dock (Run's ADR-0017): a dock lives inside one tab and would put the coach on a third of the app.

track-open.title: Track — a session is open
track-open.in: Nav bar › Track, with a session still running
track-open.note: The primary changes verb, not position.
track-open.doc: Backing out of a session leaves it open on purpose — every change is already persisted — so Track has to offer it back. The button becomes "Resume session" in the same slot rather than a second control appearing, because there is still only one thing to do here.

track-planned.title: Track — today is in the plan
track-planned.in: Nav bar › Track, with a plan that has something for today
track-planned.next: Start upper — the day's name, not "today's session"
track-planned.note: The button says what you are about to do.
track-planned.doc: When a plan has something for today the primary names it — "Start upper" — so the button says what you are about to do rather than that something exists. Derived from the plan's weekdays on the spot: a standing plan has no session rows to look up.

track-interrupted.title: Track — walked away mid-session
track-interrupted.in: Nav bar › Track, a day after a session was left open
track-interrupted.note: Yesterday's session, two sets in, still offered.
track-interrupted.doc: The case an app that only ever shows "today" gets wrong. The session is a day old and still open, and the screen offers it back rather than hiding it or quietly closing it — nothing in Lift ever ends a session on the lifter's behalf.

session-empty.title: Session — nothing in it yet
session-empty.out: Back arrow — the session stays open
session-empty.doc: Adding a movement is the primary and the lifter's own library is the quieter second. These were once the other way round, with the app's premade list as the loudest control on a blank session — which the "templates are the coach's grounding layer, not a user-facing library" decision rules out. Back is deliberately unguarded: the session is already written, and Track offers it back.

workout-library-empty.title: Your workouts — empty
workout-library-empty.out: Drag or scrim; the grab bar is the only thing that says so
workout-library-empty.note: Points at the premades — the one moment that list is the right answer.
workout-library-empty.doc: The empty state points at the premade list, which is the only moment that list is the right answer: before there is anything of your own to start from. Every sheet in the app carries a SheetHandle, because both dismiss gestures are invisible and three sheets shipped without one.

workout-library.title: Your workouts
workout-library.note: Newest first, each showing the movements it contains.
workout-library.doc: Saved sessions, most recent first, each showing its movements so a name you no longer remember is still identifiable. A workout added from a premade keeps a back-reference to it, which is how the premade list knows what you already have.

premade-library.title: Premade workouts
premade-library.next: Add one, or add a whole split
premade-library.note: Adding writes a copy into your library, not a link to the catalogue.
premade-library.doc: Adding writes a copy into your own library rather than starting the premade directly — so editing it later changes yours and not the catalogue. Adding a split adds every session in it, and anything already taken is marked.

workout-builder.title: Build a workout
workout-builder.note: The same shape a finished session is saved as.
workout-builder.doc: A name and an ordered list of movements — the same shape a finished session is saved as, because they are the same thing arrived at from two directions. Movements come from the picker, so the catalogue and its form images are reachable here too.

session.title: Session — running
session.out: Back arrow, Finish, or Discard session
session.note: Elapsed, volume, sets, movements — the four that once collided.
session.doc: The screen the app exists for. Every set is written the moment it is ticked, which is what makes back safe and an interrupted session resumable. The header's four figures were the fault found by photographing this screen rather than testing it: at 390pt they collided and read "1410 kg3".

path.note: The common path, and one tap. Weight and reps are already carried forward from the set above, so typing is the exception.
Only on completion. Un-ticking is a correction to the log, not the end of a set — so it must not start a rest.
Held in the widget, never written. This is why the resting state is unreachable without a tap, and why the harness needs startRestOnOpen to photograph it.
Not awaited by the tap. The write goes to the on-device database and returns; the network is not consulted and cannot fail here, so no spinner ever blocks a set being logged.
The device is the source of truth for a session in progress. Sync is a later, separate concern that cannot lose a set.
The recorder returns the whole updated session rather than an ack, so the screen never has to guess what changed. Finish enables itself off completedSets > 0.

exercise-picker.title: Add a movement
exercise-picker.next: Pick one, or type your own
exercise-picker.note: 266 movements with form images, and nobody had ever seen it.
exercise-picker.doc: Search the catalogue or type your own; both end as a name on the session, and the catalogue simply gets you there faster and brings a picture. It replaced a bare text field — not wrong, but it made every session start with spelling. Reachable from two screens and, until this board, addressable from neither.

swap-sheet.title: Swap a movement
swap-sheet.next: Take the replacement, or leave it
swap-sheet.note: Built on the frame every "ask for a change" sheet shares.
swap-sheet.doc: Asks the coach for a substitute and shows what it proposes against what you have actually lifted. Built on AskCoachSheet, the shared frame for every ask-for-a-change sheet — written because swapping a movement and changing a week had already drifted into two heights and two label conventions in a day.

session-long.title: Session — six movements
session-long.in: {{session}} › a template with more in it than fits
session-long.note: Three finished and collapsed to a line each.
session-long.doc: The case the collapse exists for: expanded throughout, this session is around 2,000px and the movement you are actually on is off screen. A finished movement folds to one line and reopens on a tap.

session-resting.title: Session — resting
session-resting.next: Wait, or start the next set
session-resting.note: The rest bar, over the list.
session-resting.doc: Rest starts on the tick and is never restored from disk, which is why this state can only be reached by ticking something: a rest timer resumed from storage would count time the lifter spent doing something else entirely.

session-summary.title: Summary — an ordinary session
session-summary.out: Back arrow, Back to Track, or the coach
session-summary.note: Worked hard, beat nothing — which is the common case.
session-summary.doc: Added 2026-08-25: Run had a summary and Lift finished a session by dropping you back onto Track with nothing. This fixture lands at or under every best already in the log, because matching a best is not setting one. Finish replaces rather than pushes, so back does not return to a session that has ended.

path.note: Asserts the session has ended. A summary of an open session would report no bests at all rather than reporting none honestly, so it is a programming error rather than a state to handle.
The session filters itself out of its own history. Left in, every movement would be compared against itself and could never beat anything.
A lifter who came back to the bench at the end has one movement here, not two — the best already folds every exercise of that name in the session.
Null skips the movement entirely. Epley is capped at 12 reps, so fifteens produce nothing — which is the honest answer rather than a number invented to fill the row.

path.call: Epley: weight × (1 + reps / 30), null above 12 reps
path.note: A fitted line, not a measurement. At 30 reps it claims a double. The old app capped at 30; this is stricter, because a confidently wrong best is worse than no best.
Null skips too — a movement with no history is not a best, because there is nothing to have beaten. Counting it would make a first session nothing but bests, which empties the word.
Matching a best is not setting one. A session that repeats last week's top set to the kilogram should not be told it moved.

session-summary-pb.title: Summary — a personal best
session-summary-pb.out: Back arrow, Back to Track, or the coach
session-summary-pb.note: Ten kilos is the only difference from {{session-summary}}.
session-summary-pb.doc: 95 × 5 estimates at 110.8 kg against the 105 kg already in the log. Bests are strictly greater, and a movement with no history is not a best — there is nothing to have beaten, and counting it would make a first session nothing but bests.

session-summary-short.title: Summary — a first session
session-summary-short.in: {{session}} › Finish, with nothing to compare against
session-summary-short.note: Fifteens are above Epley's cap, so it says it cannot tell.
session-summary-short.doc: The two states easiest to get wrong, at once: nothing in the log to compare against, and nothing that can be estimated from. "No estimate" is a separate fact from "nothing beat your best". The second movement was added and never worked, which is the only case where the movement count is larger than the sets explain.

save-workout.title: Name this workout
save-workout.note: Pre-filled and selected, so the common answer is one tap.
save-workout.doc: One field, pre-filled with the session's name and selected. Offered from two moments — "I can tell this is worth keeping" and "that worked" — and it moved to the summary because saving is a decision about the shape of a session made after seeing it, and until the summary existed there was nowhere to see it.

plan.title: Plan — the offer
plan.in: Nav bar › Plan, on a free account
plan.note: The paywall is the tab's empty state, not a wall in front of it.
plan.doc: The tab a free account sees. The offer is the tab's own empty state rather than a wall in front of it, so what is being sold and where it will appear are the same screen. This was hardcoded to the pitch until the entitlement was read properly.

plan-entitled.title: Plan — paid, no block yet
plan-entitled.in: Nav bar › Plan, once the entitlement reads true
plan-entitled.note: The state between paying and having anything.
plan-entitled.doc: One action, because there is only one thing that can happen next — and the paywall is gone the moment the entitlement reads true, which is what this plate is here to prove.

plan-standing.title: Plan — a training day
plan-standing.in: Nav bar › Plan, entitled, with a plan
plan-standing.next: Start today's workout, or Change the split
plan-standing.note: Monday, Upper, six movements — the density a real plan produces.
plan-standing.doc: PlanSurface hands the entitled-with-a-plan case straight to the standing plan, so the paywall screen and the plan screen are one widget getting out of its own way. Built by PlanTemplate rather than a hand-written fixture, so the density is what the app will really produce — six movements on an Upper day, not the three a fixture happens to contain.

path.note: weekdays.indexOf(date.weekday) into dayOrder. There is no calendar and no session rows — the week is a function of the date, which is why a plan never falls behind and a rest day is an answer rather than a gap.

path.call: null → onStartToday is null, not disabled
path.note: Null rather than a greyed button, because on a rest day there is genuinely nothing to start rather than something withheld.
Turns today's slots into movements with targets, worked out from what this lifter has actually lifted — and left blank where there is nothing to work it out from.

path.call: increment: 2.5 kg for a main lift, 1 kg otherwise
path.note: Different by movement class because they are different in the gym: a barbell takes the smallest pair of plates most racks have; the next dumbbell up on a lateral raise is a 20% jump nobody makes cleanly.

Resuming still wins. An open session is offered back exactly as it is for a plain start — filling a plan over the top of one somebody is halfway through would destroy the sets they had already logged.
The link from plan to session is written when the session FINISHES, not when it starts: a session opened and abandoned is not one they did.

plan-standing-rest.title: Plan — a rest day
plan-standing-rest.in: Nav bar › Plan, on a Wednesday
plan-standing-rest.doc: A rest day is an answer, not an empty state — which is the whole point of deriving the week from weekdays rather than scheduling sessions into it. Nothing is overdue, because nothing was ever booked.

coach-empty.title: Coach — nothing said yet
coach-empty.out: App bar back; a reply in flight is abandoned
coach-empty.note: A sheet over where you were, so you can still see it.
coach-empty.doc: Not a fourth destination pushed on top of the app — you can still see the surface you came from, which is the difference between asking about this and leaving to go and ask. Opening it checks the account and the entitlement before the message rather than after, so a refusal never arrives on a screen with no route to the fix.

path.note: The shell owns what opening the coach means, so both gates live in one place rather than at every call site.

path.call: if (coach == null) return          // no mark at all
path.note: The mark stays absent rather than inert when there is no server. A mark that cannot open anything is worse than no mark.
Checked before the message, not after. Sending a question and getting "sign in" back means the lifter typed something for nothing, and the refusal lands on a screen with no route to the fix.
The free tier is sent to the offer rather than shown a refusal — the tab whose empty state IS the pitch.
The server enforces both gates again before spending anything. This only stops a round trip that cannot succeed.
Tall enough that a conversation is not a peephole, short enough that the surface behind stays visible. Root navigator, or the nav bar draws over the composer.
A scrim, not a blackout. Seeing where you came from is the difference between a sheet and a screen.

coach.title: Coach — the opening line
coach.note: "Your bench has not moved in three weeks."
coach.doc: The coach opens on an observation drawn from the log rather than a greeting, because a blank conversation puts the work of starting it on the lifter. Glass over the surface underneath — the one presentation GlassSurface says does not work on flat charcoal, which is why every coach preview goes through the real sheet.

coach-resumed.title: Coach — resumed
coach-resumed.in: The mark, on a conversation already going
coach-resumed.note: Worth checking against a real account before trusting it.
coach-resumed.doc: Reopening on what was already said — the state a returning lifter is actually in, and the one that did not exist until the transcript was wired. Run's one live conversation is keyed by a legacy client-generated id rather than the one its client and edge function both use, and resume reads empty for exactly that reason.

coach-history.title: Previous conversations
coach-history.doc: A conversation ends after thirty minutes of silence (ADR-0002), so the coach no longer opens on whatever was last said however long ago — which is what let it read a month-old exchange as current. The cost is that a lifter stops finding last week's conversation waiting for them, so it is kept, and it is here: the same words, in a place that says plainly they are over. Rows lead with the opening line rather than the date, because a column of dates is a filing cabinet.

coach-history-empty.title: Nothing kept yet
coach-history-empty.note: Empty and loading are different states.
coach-history-empty.doc: Says what will fill it rather than that it is empty. The distinction that matters here is against the loading state: a list that draws this message while the read is outstanding tells a lifter with ten conversations that they have none, which is why the two are separate rather than one falsy check.

coach-past.title: One, read back
coach-past.note: Read-only by construction: there is no composer.
coach-past.doc: The whole conversation, not the window {{coach-resumed}} shows — that one answers "what does the coach still have in mind", this one answers "what was said", and a read-back truncated at twenty turns would silently cut the thing somebody opened it to re-read. Nothing here loads it back into the live conversation: reopening an old transcript to write into it is exactly the endless chat sessions exist to end, and the footer says so rather than leaving somebody hunting for a box that is not there.

coach-limit.title: Coach — out of turns
coach-limit.note: Names the limit rather than failing vaguely.
coach-limit.doc: The server enforces the limit too — this is the client stopping a round trip that cannot succeed, not the rule itself.

coach-eval-jump.title: Coach — "should I try 140?"
coach-eval-jump.note: An eval scenario, rendered where a person would read it.
coach-eval-jump.doc: One of the situations supabase/evals/scenarios.ts puts the coach in, on screen so the rule can be judged as a person reads it rather than as a verdict in a table. A rule that looks right in a spec and wrong in a bubble is wrong.

coach-eval-joint-pain.title: Coach — three weeks of knee pain
coach-eval-joint-pain.note: The refusal that has to be a refusal.
coach-eval-joint-pain.doc: The coach declines to diagnose, says so plainly, and still does the part that is its job — leaving squats out of next week either way. This is the eval where a hedge would be worse than a refusal.

plan-review-after.title: Post-session review — asked
plan-review-after.doc: Adapting a week had no subject once plans stopped having weeks, so what the feature was for moved here: the coach reads what happened and asks, and the lifter's own answer is what changes the next session.

plan-review-answered.title: Post-session review — answered
plan-review-answered.note: Holds the weight, says why, then raises what you did not ask about.
plan-review-answered.doc: Two sessions at the same weight is not a stall — the coach holds rather than adds, and explains that. Then it raises the thing the lifter did not ask about: a lateral raise that has not moved in six sessions.

intake-1-days.title: Days a week
intake-1-days.out: App bar back — blocked while a turn is in flight
intake-1-days.next: Tap an option, or answer in your own words
intake-1-days.note: First, because it decides the split outright.
intake-1-days.doc: Days decides the split outright, which is why it leads — the order is by leverage rather than convention. It is also the one question with no way past it: a plan cannot be built without knowing how often somebody trains, so this is the only field the flow marks required.

intake-2-equipment.title: Equipment
intake-2-equipment.out: App bar back — blocked while a turn is in flight
intake-2-equipment.next: Tap an option, or answer in your own words
intake-2-equipment.note: Decides whether the movements are possible at all.
intake-2-equipment.doc: Second because it decides whether the movements are possible at all. Everything after this is a constraint on a plan that already has a shape. The last row is the way out, and it is a row rather than a separate control because declining is an answer — it goes into the transcript the coach reads back.

intake-3-injuries.title: Injuries
intake-3-injuries.out: App bar back — blocked while a turn is in flight
intake-3-injuries.next: Tap an option, or answer in your own words
intake-3-injuries.note: A hard constraint, and its own way of being declined.
intake-3-injuries.doc: "Nothing to work around" is the only option offered, and it is the skip as well as an answer — a real reply rather than a refusal, so a "prefer not to say" underneath it would be two rows for one intention.

intake-4-goal.title: The goal
intake-4-goal.out: App bar back — blocked while a turn is in flight
intake-4-goal.next: Tap an option, or answer in your own words
intake-4-goal.note: Fourth, because it moves rep ranges and little else.
intake-4-goal.doc: Most apps open with this question and then do nothing with the answer. It moves rep ranges at the margin, which is worth exactly fourth place. Three options rather than six: "lose weight" and "gain weight" are nutrition goals whose training answer is the same block as "build muscle", so offering them separately costs a decision and buys nothing.

intake-11-ready.title: Ready to build
intake-11-ready.out: App bar back — blocked while a turn is in flight
intake-11-ready.note: The options stop, because there is nothing left to ask.
intake-11-ready.doc: Nothing left to ask, so the options stop and the button appears — which is the whole of the summary. It appears the moment a block could be built rather than when the coach decides the conversation is over, and there is one definition of "enough": every field answered or declined, in intake_flow.dart. PlanIntake carried a second one that disagreed in both directions, and it is gone. Q11 rather than Q5 because codes are pinned in the data — the three body questions that held 5, 6 and 7 were cut, and nothing that survived them moves.

intake-9-split.title: The split it chose
intake-9-split.next: Take it, or ask for another
intake-9-split.note: Named by the coach with its reason attached.
intake-9-split.doc: Not picked from a list of three: the app checks what a plan does, not what it is called, and the name arrives with the reasoning that produced it.
intake-9-split.flag: The coach sheet is real; this conversation is not — the split is named on {{plan-standing}}, not in chat.

intake-10-swap.title: Swap before starting
intake-10-swap.note: The capability is real; only this entry point is not.
intake-10-swap.doc: Changing a movement before the block begins, which in the shipping app happens afterwards from the plan screen's "Change the split".
intake-10-swap.flag: The coach sheet is real, and so is the swap — but it happens after the block starts, from {{plan-standing}}.

profile.title: Profile
profile.next: Open photos, settings, or the log
profile.note: Six figures and the year grid, back from the old app.
profile.doc: The log, behind. Its heading used to announce itself in the same voice as its own subsections — which a side-by-side with Run caught and a test never would.

profile-empty.title: Profile — nothing logged
profile-empty.in: Nav bar › Profile, on a new account
profile-empty.note: Shows what it will track, rather than apologising.
profile-empty.doc: Run's Profile still collapses to "No runs yet." — the same complaint you made about Lift, still open there.

photos-empty.title: Progress photos — empty
photos-empty.note: The empty state has to teach the cadence.
photos-empty.doc: One stream per pose, one photo per week. A photo app that accepts one a day teaches the wrong habit — a body does not change between Tuesday and Wednesday — so the empty state explains the rhythm rather than just inviting a tap.

photos.title: Progress photos
photos.next: Open a pose, or add this week's
photos.note: Grey tiles are the browser, not the app.
photos.doc: Every pose, this week first. Imagery needs the emulator; this plate is here for the grid, the chrome and the week labels.

photo-source.title: Camera or gallery
photo-source.out: Drag, scrim, or the grab bar
photo-source.next: Take a photo, or choose one
photo-source.note: One of the three sheets that shipped with no way out.
photo-source.doc: Asked every time rather than remembered: the gallery is how you backfill a photo you already took and the camera is how you do this week, and neither is the default. The 2026-08-08 exit sweep found this sheet shipping with no dismiss affordance at all.

photo-series.title: One pose, every week
photo-series.note: Two missed weeks, left as gaps.
photo-series.doc: A grid rather than a list, because the comparison is the content. The missed fortnight is left as a gap rather than closed up: a sequence that hides its holes claims a consistency the lifter did not have.

photo-actions.title: Photo actions
photo-actions.out: Drag, scrim, or the grab bar
photo-actions.note: The grab bar is load-bearing here more than anywhere.
photo-actions.doc: Skipping keeps the photo and takes it out of the sequence; the subtitle says so, because "skip" beside "delete" has to be unambiguous. The loudest control on this sheet deletes something that cannot be retaken, and it opens on a tap.

photo-delete-confirm.title: Delete this photo?
photo-delete-confirm.doc: There is no copy anywhere else, and a photo of your own body from eight months ago cannot be retaken. "Keep it" against "Delete", which is the pairing every confirmation in both apps uses.

series-playback.title: The sequence, playing
series-playback.out: App bar back; the timer is cancelled in dispose
series-playback.note: The only thing progress photos are actually for.
series-playback.doc: In-app playback, not a video export — the old app encoded an MP4 through a native module per OS so it could be shared, and this is the part that does the actual work of showing a lifter their own change, without any of that. Speed is adjustable because a two-photo series and a fifty-photo one want very different ones.

path.note: Excluded frames are already gone by the time this screen has the series. Filtering here would put the same rule in two places and let them disagree.
Pressing play on a finished sequence means "again", not "nothing".
Fast enough to read as change rather than a slideshow, slow enough to see each week. Adjustable because a two-photo series and a fifty-photo one want very different speeds.
It stops at the end rather than looping. A loop would make it ambient wallpaper; this is something you watch once and think about.
Touching the scrubber stops playback rather than fighting it. Two things moving the same index is the classic media-player bug.
The one line that makes back safe here. Without it the timer keeps calling setState on a disposed widget, which is the failure docs/navigation.md records this screen as clean on.

settings.title: Settings — signed out
settings.next_note: units apply as they change, not on close
settings.note: Device-first units, so they survive a launch with no account.
settings.doc: The device half is what makes units survive a launch at all, since tracking needs no sign-in; the account half is what makes them agree with Run. A change here reaches Track and Profile without either reloading, because the shell holds them.

settings-signed-in.title: Settings — signed in
settings-signed-in.next: Sync, sign out, or open Coach
settings-signed-in.note: The account section fills in and the memory becomes reachable.
settings-signed-in.doc: Memory is deliberately separate from the coach itself: somebody who has stopped paying should still be able to read what was stored about them and delete it.

account-signed-out.title: Account — nine waiting
account-signed-out.in: {{settings}} › with training in one place only
account-signed-out.note: The argument for an account, made with a number.
account-signed-out.doc: Nothing here blocks logging — the local database has everything and the rows stay pending. It reports rather than reassures, because discovering that your training is on one device only is worst after losing a phone.

account-synced.title: Account — up to date
account-synced.note: A time rather than a status word.
account-synced.doc: "Synced" is only useful if you know when. This card read the wall clock until 2026-08-27, so on a pinned fixture it said a three-minute-old sync was 20 days ago — and got a day worse every day.

path.note: Owned by the shell rather than by Settings, so the result survives Settings being closed and Track sees the refreshed log.
One at a time. Two overlapping runs would race on the same pending rows and report each other's outcome.

A failure comes back as a report with outcome unavailable, not an exception. The local database is the source of truth and nothing is lost by a sync that did not happen, so there is nothing here worth an error state.

path.call: → push what is pending, pull what is missing
path.note: Restore only ever adds. A pull cannot delete local training, which is why signing in on a new phone is safe and signing out leaves everything alone.
The count is re-read rather than decremented from what the report claims — the server decides what actually landed.
Rough on purpose: "3 min ago" answers "did that work"; a timestamp to the second does not. Takes an injected clock so a pinned fixture reads correctly.

coach-memory.title: What the coach remembers
coach-memory.doc: Written as what the coach would say about you rather than as a table, which would imply a precision it does not have. Readable and clearable without an entitlement.

coach-memory-empty.title: Memory — nothing formed yet
coach-memory-empty.note: A real state, not an error.
coach-memory-empty.doc: Memory is formed from conversations, so a lifter who has not had one has nothing here and nothing to do about it.

coach-memory-error.title: Memory — will not load
coach-memory-error.doc: "Nothing stored" and "could not read what is stored" are different answers to "what do you know about me", and collapsing them would be the worse kind of wrong.

credits.title: Credits
credits.note: The one plate here with nothing to do on it.
credits.doc: Licences and attribution for the exercise catalogue and its images. A dead end by design.

track-backup-failed.title: Track — backup failed
track-backup-failed.in: Nav bar › Track, after a backup run that could not finish
track-backup-failed.next: Try again, or carry on training
track-backup-failed.note: A pill only when something needs the lifter, never a status bar.
track-backup-failed.doc: Backup runs at checkpoints (launch, return to the app, Finish, a changed workout), never while logging, and retries on its own. The pill appears only when a run has actually failed and says what to do; a healthy backup is silent on Track, because training is the point of this tab and syncing is not.

track-backup-refused.title: Track — a workout refused
track-backup-refused.in: Nav bar › Track, after the server refused one workout
track-backup-refused.note: One refused workout never holds up the rest.
track-backup-refused.doc: Each workout goes up on its own. One the server refuses is set aside with its reason and waits for an edit, while everything else carries on backing up, so a single bad row cannot block a lifter's whole history.

workout-preview.title: A saved workout, before starting
workout-preview.in: {{workout-library}} › a workout, or the Track row
workout-preview.note: What it holds, set by set, before the clock starts.
workout-preview.doc: Starting from here lays every set out with the reps aimed for and the weight lifted last time, so a set that matches is one tap on the tick. Weight is never stored in a workout: it comes from the log, which is what makes the fill honest.

workout-preview-blocked.title: A saved workout, with a session open
workout-preview-blocked.next: Finish or discard the open session first
workout-preview-blocked.note: Start says why it cannot, rather than overwriting anything.
workout-preview-blocked.doc: An open session is always offered back, never replaced: filling a workout over one somebody is halfway through would destroy sets they had logged, which is the worst thing this app could do.

workout-editor.title: Editing a saved workout
workout-editor.next: Change sets and rep targets, reorder, remove
workout-editor.note: The builder's screen, titled for the workout it edits.
workout-editor.doc: Sets from 1 to 20 and reps up to 200. A workout holds the set count and the rep target, never a weight. It also learns on its own at Finish (see {{session-summary-lesson}}), so this screen is for the changes a session cannot teach.

session-rest-over.title: Session — rest over
session-rest-over.out: Done, or tick the next set
session-rest-over.note: Counts up past zero, in green: how long the rest actually was.
session-rest-over.doc: Added 2026-09-29 from the competitor research, which found a timer people cannot trust to be the commonest complaint about every app in the category. Past zero it keeps counting (+0:42) rather than freezing at 0:00. With the phone locked or the app in the background, the buzz comes as a system notification at the rest's fixed end, naming the next set; the app withdraws it on return, so there is never a second buzz. Each movement remembers its own rest length.

exercise-picker-replace.title: Swap a movement, by hand
exercise-picker-replace.in: {{session}} › the swap icon, without the coach
exercise-picker-replace.next: Tap one: it replaces the movement and closes
exercise-picker-replace.note: The swap icon used to exist only for coached lifters.
exercise-picker-replace.doc: The same picker as {{exercise-picker}}, in replace mode: titled for the movement being swapped, and one tap chooses and closes. The replacement takes the sets still to do, their target reps and the new movement's weight from last time. Logged sets stay where they are, under the old name, because they were lifted. A coached lifter gets {{swap-sheet}} instead.

reorder-sheet.title: Reorder movements
reorder-sheet.in: {{session}} › Reorder movements, at the foot of the list
reorder-sheet.next: Drag by the handle, then Done
reorder-sheet.note: The bench is taken, so incline goes first.
reorder-sheet.doc: The recorder could always reorder; nothing on screen reached it until 2026-09-29. A sheet of one-line rows rather than drag handles on the cards, because the cards are tall and full of fields, the wrong surface to start a long-press drag on. Shown only once a session has two movements.

session-summary-lesson.title: Summary — the workout learns
session-summary-lesson.in: {{session}} › Finish, started from a saved workout
session-summary-lesson.note: Remove Cable Fly once and it stays removed.
session-summary-lesson.doc: A session started from a saved workout teaches it at Finish: movements removed, movements added and done, and set counts. Never weights. The change applies straight away with Undo beside it, so a lifter never has to rebuild a template by hand.

session-summary-offline.title: Summary — saved on this phone
session-summary-offline.next: Nothing; it backs up later on its own
session-summary-offline.note: True and calm: the session is safe, the upload is pending.
session-summary-offline.doc: Every set is on the phone the moment it is ticked. The line under the totals says so rather than showing a spinner, and backup retries at 30 seconds, 2 minutes, 10 minutes, then hourly.

session-summary-backed-up.title: Summary — backed up
session-summary-backed-up.note: Said only once the server has it.
session-summary-backed-up.doc: The line changes to Backed up only when a backup run has completed after this session finished, so it can never claim something that has not happened.

purchase-sheet.title: Choose a tier
purchase-sheet.out: Drag or scrim; closes itself after a purchase
purchase-sheet.next: Subscribe to Coach or Premium Coach
purchase-sheet.note: Both tiers buyable. Before, the table showed Premium and the button bought Coach.
purchase-sheet.doc: Where money moves, and where Guideline 3.1.2 is met in one place: each tier's name, period and store price, the renewal terms in the store's own words (Apple's here, Play's on Android), working links to the terms and privacy policy, and Restore. Prices are the store's strings; the app never writes one. Signed out, it asks for an account instead of money, because a purchase with no account behind it unlocks nothing.

history.title: Every session
history.doc: Profile shows the last five and nothing led past them, so a session from last month counted in every total and could never be looked at, let alone fixed. This is the way in to all of them, with the not-backed-up mark on any row still waiting.

session-past.title: A past session
session-past.next: Edit session, or Delete session with Undo
session-past.note: The summary's own layout, dated, with Edit and Delete.
session-past.doc: Its bests are the ones it set at the time. Delete is soft with Undo, and the session leaves every total at once; the deletion also reaches other devices.

session-editing.title: Fixing a past session
session-editing.note: The session screen itself, aimed at a session that already happened.
session-editing.doc: Same rows, same limits, same input rules, because it is the same screen with a recorder aimed at the old session. No clock and no rest; the date and length stay what they were, and unticked sets go at Done as they do at Finish.

account-problems.title: Account — what backup could not do
account-problems.in: {{settings}}, when a run failed or a workout was refused
account-problems.next: Sync now, or edit the refused workout
account-problems.note: Every refusal listed with its reason.
account-problems.doc: Where {{track-backup-refused}} sends the lifter. A refused workout is named with the server's reason and waits for an edit; a failed run says when it will try again. Settings also gained a Workout section on 2026-09-29 with the rest-alert switch, shown on {{settings}} and {{settings-signed-in}}.

edges.label: the mark in the top bar
